newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
White sugar futures in London ended lower with front month March losing $2.00 to close at $297.90. May gave up $1.90 to close at $297.70.
News that the Philippines plans to export 200,000 tonnes of refined sugar to reduce its mounting stocks, could depress prices on Tuesday.

On the positive side is the possibility that Iraq will be in the market for significant quantities of white sugar after final agreement has been reached on a deal with the United Nations allowing the country to sell oil in return for much-needed food supplies, including sugar.

Iraq does not publish any import figures but it is known that it gets most of its sugar from Turkey and via Jordan. Smaller quantities come from Germany, Belgium, Brazil and Thailand. It is also possible that Iraq imported some Ukrainian sugar. Imports in recent years were most likely between 300,000 and 400,000 tonnes annually, which compares to 600,000-700,000 tonnes before the UN sanctions.

In New York raw sugar futures fell to support at 10.30 cents/lb as trade scale-down buying kept the contract from accumulating additional losses. However, a move below support could trigger aggressive speculative selling and pressure the March contract to major support at 10.23 cents/lb, the recent low made December 3.
Many analysts expect world prices to remain under pressure.

ISO - The International Sugar Organization (ISO) has marginally adjusted its world production estimate for 1996/97 to 123.6 million tonnes, raw value, down from 123.79 million tonnes previously. The revised figure would exceed consumption by nearly 3 million tonnes, the ISO said. In its earlier estimate of the world 1996/97 balance issued in October, the ISO pegged consumption at 121.29 million tonnes, leaving a statistical surplus of 2.50 million tonnes.

The ISO said that Russian and Chinese sugar demand will be pivotal for any world price recovery before spring 1997 but the overhanging surplus will still be a bearish element. The ISO added that it would appear that without Russian and Chinese purchases it would be difficult to reverse the existing mid-term bearish trend, at least until spring 1997. This would be when new crop outputs and the intentions of southern hemisphere exporters became clear, it said.

CANDADA - Sugar imports in September 1996 amounted to 105,856 tonnes, raw value, up on last year's 45,024 tonnes. This brought total imports in 1995/96 up to 1.160 million tonnes against 1.013 million tonnes in 1994/95 and 1.212 million tonnes in 1993/94. Major countries of origin in 1995/96 were Australia with 714,180 tonnes raws against 596,134 tonnes and Cuba with 144,744 tonnes, up from 136,930 tonnes.

New on the list of suppliers to Canada were Brazil with 81,494 tonnes, Guatemala with 61,417 tonnes, Colombia with 57,361 tonnes and South Africa with 17,980 tonnes. The largest white sugar supplier continued to be the USA shipping 29,718 tonnes, sharply down from 116,001 tonnes in 1994/95.

JAMAICA - Sugar production in June 1996 amounted to 27,200 tonnes, raw value, up from last year's 17,771 tonnes. This brought cumulative production in the first eight months of 1995/96 (November/June) up to 226,135 tonnes against 197,403 tonnes in the corresponding period the previous year. Total production 1994/95 hit 211,539 tonnes against 220,350 tonnes in 1993/94.

SWITZERLAND - Sugar imports in October 1996, the first month of 1996/97 (October/September), amounted to 10,113 tonnes, raw value, down from last year's 15,262 tonnes. Total imports in 1995/96 reached 169,873 tonnes, compared to 155,620 tonnes in 1994/95. The major country of origin in October 1996 was Germany with 6,799 tonnes whites, down from last year's 9,274 tonnes. Swiss import requirements will be sharply lower in 1996/97 due to a considerably improved domestic harvest.

The state-run Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) has delayed a decision on bids received for the import of 50,000 tonnes of sugar. A TCP official said that the corporation had sent a report on the bidding to a government committee which will discuss the issue on Thursday.

He said the report contained a recommendation that Pakistan buy sugar only from the 1996/97 (July/June) crop and not accept sugar from the 1995/96 crop as offered by one Indian bidder. The TCP received 9 bids to supply 50,000 tonnes of crystal white sugar for shipment by December 31.
The Philippines plans to export 200,000 tonnes of refined sugar onto the world market to reduce its mounting stocks, Sugar Regulatory Administration chief Wilson Gamboa said.
